issues.legal_issue: A writ petition should not be dismissed as involving disputed title when the claimant’s title is admitted and the dispute concerns the public authority’s right to resume the property.
material_facts: The claimant’s title as lessee was not disputed by the State.
The dispute concerned whether the State was entitled to resume the land under the lease.
The High Court dismissed the writ petition on the ground that disputed questions of title required a civil suit.
issues.conclusion: The High Court had no justification for dismissing the writ petition in limine on the ground that a disputed question of title was involved; its judgment was set aside and the matter remanded.
issues.legal_principle: Article 226 provides supervisory jurisdiction over public authorities and tribunals to ensure that they obey the law and act within their jurisdiction. A dispute about the authority to resume property is not, by itself, a disputed question of title when the claimant’s title is admitted. State of Orissa v. Ramchandra was distinguished because the parties there disputed the character of the grants and the nature of the title.

predicates.writ_dismissal_appeal: A party appeals after a court dismisses that party’s writ petition.
predicates.claimant_title_admitted: The public authority does not dispute the claimant’s title to the property.
predicates.dispute_concerns_resumption_authority: The dispute concerns whether the public authority has the right to resume the property, rather than who holds title.

issues.definition: When a party appeals the dismissal of a writ petition, the claimant’s title is admitted, and the dispute concerns the authority to resume the property, the petition is not dismissed as involving disputed title.

issues.legal_issue: A writ petition is not barred as a mere contractual claim when it challenges public-authority action and raises important constitutional or other public-law issues.
material_facts: The claimant challenged the State’s resumption of leased property and the executive action to take possession.
The claimant raised issues about whether the State had acquired the relevant rights and whether executive authorities could forcibly interfere with property without legal authority.
The claim therefore raised important constitutional and public-law issues and was not merely an attempt to enforce a contractual right.
The High Court held that the claimant’s remedy was a civil suit and that a writ petition was not maintainable.
issues.conclusion: The writ petition could not be rejected on the basis that it sought only to enforce contractual rights; the High Court’s judgment was set aside and the petition remanded for decision in accordance with law.
issues.legal_principle: Article 226 provides a public-law remedy against violations of rights by the State or statutory authorities and enables the High Court to ensure that public authorities remain within their jurisdiction. Basappa v. Nagappa was cited for the application in Indian law of the essential principles of prerogative writs. The Court did not decide the underlying entitlement to resume the property.

rule.if: writ_proceeding and public_authority_action_challenged and important_public_law_issues_raised and not merely_contractual_enforcement

predicates.writ_proceeding: A claimant brings a proceeding seeking writ relief against public-authority action.
predicates.public_authority_action_challenged: The claimant challenges action taken by a public authority affecting the claimant’s rights.
predicates.important_public_law_issues_raised: The claimant raises important constitutional or other public-law issues about the authority’s action.
predicates.merely_contractual_enforcement: The claimant’s proceeding seeks only to enforce a contractual right.

issues.definition: A writ proceeding challenging public-authority action and raising important public-law issues is not rejected as merely contractual when it seeks more than enforcement of a contractual right.
